utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. This witness enjoys certain protection -- protective measures, in particular this is Witness T-61, pseudonym and image distortion. Could we show this document to the witness, please. I'd like to tender this document as a Defence exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes D288, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We should continue in private session, please, in order to go through the witness's particulars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain to the Judges something that has to do with the beginning of the conflict. What did you have to do as part of your work in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically my current tasks, those of a surgeon, the only thing that changed was the structure of the patients. Before we dealt with different pathology, mainly traffic accidents, but now we had many wounded people. I was the head of a team of 12 to 16 people who worked on the patients coming to the hospital mainly due to war activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which type of wound -- of the wounded prevailed at first, let's say early 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can start with April 1992, if this is what you have in mind. What prevailed then were wounded people which began around the 6th or the 7th of April and lasted until June, some three or four months, I would say late June. It was particularly heavy in early June and many people were wounded at that time. There were both civilians and soldiers. Some of them would come in in full JNA uniform at first, at the beginning of the war; and later we saw many wounded in camouflage uniforms, some in full uniforms, some with only parts of uniforms, some wearing civilian clothes or a mixture. This is what situation was like in terms of the type of clothing, but these were mainly younger people. At the beginning of the war, another interesting thing is that particularly until the 10th or the 12th or the 15th of April there were many wounded who were captured JNA soldiers. These were children, 19 or 20 years of age, because that was the time to serve your military term. They were basically abandoned by their officers in the facilities where they were without electricity or water, and then they would try and go out into town. Many got wounded then. Some even caused some self-inflicted wounds in order to be admitted into the hospital. Many of them were awaited by the Patriotic League, who would wait for them in front of the hospital, and I don't know what their fate would be as of that moment onwards. The rumour had it that they would usually be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about later, the type of the wounded as time passed by compared to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 50 or 60 per cent of the wounded were usually soldiers. 30 to 40 per cent were civilians, out of which 5 to 8 per cent were children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are now talking about the hospital which was in the area of responsibility which was under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first they were called the Patriotic League, then the Green Berets, and then the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that is the area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until early January 1994, you worked in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My last working day, as I said, was the 2nd of January, 1994. I worked regularly on my -- at my duties until that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a physician, what do you think of your work at the time? Did you change your modus operandi as opposed to the time before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Physicians don't change their attitude towards their work; we only adjust to the conditions. We operated on all people equally, among which there was the minister of health, Dr. Izetbegovic's physician who was wounded due to a fall he sustained. I operated on him since I had the most experience, and they wanted to have the most experienced operator. Juka Prazina was operated on as well, who at the time was a powerful figure in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, where is all this taking us, all this detail? Please lead the witness to evidence that is more relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a witness who will testify to certain combat actions that had to do with that area, but also he's in a good position as the doctor whom we heard before, Dr. Pejic, to testify about other things. There was a serious discussion on the relevance with that witness, and we had to forward our written submission. This doctor worked in that hospital, which was in the AOR of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Could we please move into private session or closed session to -- in order to discuss this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To discuss what? You mean evidence from the witness or is it submissions which you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to mention a certain piece of information about this witness, and then we can immediately return into open session. I wanted to state another piece of information that has to do something with his testimony which might potentially identify him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you also testified in the Galic case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified in another proceedings conducted in Trebinje back in 1996. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was Judge Stevic or Stanic who summoned me to the Trebinje court. I provided a statement and a testimony which lasted for about an hour or an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I received a document from the Prosecutor which is 65 ter document 3388. It has been partially translated. I would kindly ask for the document to be shown to the witness, since I wanted to put the translated part to him. I also wanted to ask him a few things that he testified about before that investigating judge in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have it in Serbian, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to page 6, please, in B/C/S, and this is the page that we see in the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at paragraph 2, please, and if you can read the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I have witnessed shells falling into the Kosevo Hospital area on many occasions."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second, please. The interpreter is not able to hear the witness very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start from the beginning. "I have witnessed shells falling onto the Kosevo Hospital area on many occasions. They hit the traumatology clinic twice in my immediate vicinity. However, this always happened after repeated fire by the Muslim army just below the traumatology clinic, where a school of some sort was located and we would always take shelter later on as soon as they started to fire on the Serb positions. This clinic was some 15 metres away from the faculty of civil engineering, where this school was located." And I have to add something. The institute for construction material was at this distance. The faculty was about 10 to 30 -- or 10 to 50 metres behind that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what weapons did the Muslim army fire from the vicinity of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As part of the university --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would just like to make the point -- I'm not raising a strong objection at this point, but I would just like to make the point that this testimony was not something that was mentioned in the 65 ter summary at all, although of course we were aware this witness had testified in the Galic case and have reviewed that testimony. But this was not -- the nature of weapons that may or may not have been in the vicinity of Kosevo Hospital was not something that was referred to in his 65 ter summary; it was something that was brought up in his Galic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I hear the submission. Continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Judges in more details which weapons were fired from the vicinity of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the weapons, these were two small tanks, camouflaged, and they moved in the yard among four buildings that were there in that complex near the faculty, and they mainly fired in the direction of Poljine, which is where the Serbian army was east -- to the east. It was in the area called -- that we called Jezero and farther off. Usually what happened was that after two or three firings from the same weapons, we would take shelter in a different part of the building because this part of the building facing the faculty was usually hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here on the same page, a little bit lower down, you mentioned the Patriotic League that was in a building. Can you please read the last paragraph of that same page. Yes, you can read that. There is a translation for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Immediately at the beginning of the war" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "There was also a command of the Patriotic League in the basement and on the ground floor of the Faculty of Stomatology and the clinic and in most of the schools and kindergartens that I know of in the vicinity of the Kosevo Hospital. The commander of the staff at the stomatology clinic was Juka Prazina, and I do not know who the staff commanders at the other places that were mentioned were."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These schools, these hospitals, what were they turned into, can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the following way --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please wait for my question to be completely transcribed, otherwise we're not going to get anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the dentistry clinic to look at the wife of Juka Prazina who was injured. He asked me to do that because I performed surgery on him in February of that year, following injuries in a fight. The basement area of the building was barricaded with timber and sandbags or bags filled with earth, and the entrance for us staff was the side entrance and everything was under guard. The kindergarten just underneath the medical faculty where my friends lived nearby was full of soldiers. I don't know the names. I don't know the names of the command particularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 4 on the screen, please. There is no translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we go further, can we just confirm whether we're talking about the period of 1992, 1993, 19 -- or some point in time in 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What year is this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the question of the soldiers being in these buildings, this went on throughout the whole war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, I would submit it's irrelevant because we have no indication as to the basis of the witness's knowledge in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't make it irrelevant. It goes to a different issue of whether it is believable and reliable. But let us know, Witness, what is the basis of your knowledge in this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was at the dentistry clinic twice, and the situation both times was the way that I described it just now. One time I was next to the kindergarten that I mentioned and I saw what I described. The same thing was at the Kosevsko hill school --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last part of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you just repeat the last part of what you said; the interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same situation was in the elementary school of Kosevsko Brdo, Kosevo hill, where the army was. I know that because my younger daughter went to this school, of course before the war. I went to work -- when I went to work, I often passed by this school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned the kindergarten in your testimony. Can you briefly tell us what you know about the kindergarten, which was used as a kindergarten up to a certain point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a kindergarten until the beginning of the war; after that, no children went to the kindergarten. The kindergarten was located just below the Mosa Pijade Street, that was its name before the war, and that's near the medical faculty. Passing by the kindergarten, I have to mention this once, I saw that there was soldiers inside and that there was a guard posted outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now in your testimony, as well as your testimony in the Galic case, you spoke about the suffering of people and some of your friends. Can you briefly tell us what you know about that during the period you were in the hospital and worked there until the beginning of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about the suffering of Serbs and Muslims --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please wait for my whole question to be typed out before you begin your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about the suffering of both Serbs and Muslims. I would like to speak about the late Professor Milutin Najdanovic who went -- who retired just before the war. He lived near the Kosevo Hospital in a neighbourhood of the same name, Kosevo. A group of Muslim police, special police, called Crna, took him out of his apartment one evening in front of his wife, daughter, and granddaughter, and 50 metres away from his apartment they killed him. He was found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, let us hear Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I'm rising on the point of relevance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I would tend to agree with you, unless Mr. Tapuskovic is able to persuade me otherwise. Can you persuade me, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are matters in the area of responsibility at the time of the command of Dragomir Milosevic were not happening. These were events that were in any case of significant influence on the decision of people to maintain their positions so that these things would just -- would not happen just like that, for no reason. That is one of the elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not relevant. We have said time and again that evidence of Serb suffering is not in and of itself relevant. You must be able to link it to some issue in the indictment. Move on to another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness just said both Serbs and Muslims. He said that specifically. I'm not insisting on Serbs. He said Serbs and Muslims experienced the same things. This is what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It doesn't make any difference. That particular piece of evidence is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just say one more sentence, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not on this matter. Move on to another area of the witness's evidence that is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall any events relating to gun-fire connected to the area of responsibility under the command of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was shooting in the town throughout the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in French it was translated as "artillery fire." I mentioned infantry, gun-fire, so gun-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the transcript it is: "Do you recall any events relating to gun-fire ..." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague was listening to the transcript in French, and there they said "artillery fire," but if in English -- in English it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, can you please answer if you personally noticed or experienced anything like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that there was firing in town the whole time. Of course we heard gun-fire more because it was closer. On one occasion I was with my wife at the Adra benevolence society, and it's close to the railway station. There were about 80 to 120 people in a column there waiting for assistance that was being delivered by name, but aid was delivered also to those who did not put their names down for that from the same humanitarian organisation. There was some gun-fire then in my opinion and according to the sound it came from the Energoinvest building. The people fled. Some threw themselves on the ground. I hid behind a wall, and I saw that from the one-floor-but-last of the Energoinvest building there was a white smoke. And judging by the direction of the sound, we understood that that's where the fire came from. I was lucky at another time, also in the summer of 1993, I think that that's when it was, maybe in the middle of summer. I was walking on the square in front of the railway station, and in front of me some 2 or 3 metres a bullet hit the asphalt. And I walked fast and then another one fell behind me. Then I jumped behind a building and I could see two or three shots. It all came from the area of Marin Dvor and earlier we heard that there was certain activity, firing activity, from a high-rise building near the technical school. And from the place where I was, the building was maybe some 3 to 350 metres away as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That location at Marin Dvor and the building you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Energoinvest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were in whose territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened in early January. Until then you worked as a physician. What followed in the beginning of January 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the 3rd and 4th of January, during the night, around 2.00 in the morning, the police knocked on my door, at least that's how they introduced themselves. I opened the door. I was alone. Five policemen entered. One held a torch-light turned towards my face, and another couple of policemen were holding me at gun point. The other two or searching the apartment. The whole thing may have lasted some 30 seconds. I was taken downstairs to the vehicle they had and was taken to the apartment of Dr. Ivan Sabljak. Then both of us were taken to Dr. Nemanja Veljkov's apartment. Since he wasn't home, we were then taken to the hospital and then to the police station. From that moment on we were detained. Three days after that, Ivan Sabljak's father hanged himself; he was also a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain the Judges what the reason was for your arrest. Did they tell you anything about it? Were there any proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We don't know what the real reason was. It wasn't explained to us at the moment of our arrest. While we were in the jail and when we received an indictment, it read that we were accused of committing genocide, of evading to serve the military service, and to do our work obligation. We were also accused with collaborating with the enemy, which means with the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of genocide, did they explain it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the prosecutor, but Fahija Karkanj an attorney, explained it to me, he shared my prison cell with me. He said what they thought genocide was, when any assembly took place which had more than three people in one place, they accused us of preparing an escape through the sewage shaft, which by the way does not exist. We were simply collected at our homes and there was something reported in the media cut out by my brother who showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop, please. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit that this testimony is not relevant to the charges against Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just explain the relevance, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the terror aimed at the civilians in Sarajevo, permanent terror, because people were detained for no reason. That was the terror in its true meaning: Such murders and arrests without justification. I believe in the overall context it is of great significance, since we are discussing here the situation in which Dragomir Milosevic is charged with terrorising under the circumstances when he merely had to respond to enemy activity during heavy offensives. The true terror in the literal meaning of the word, as interpreted by the entire world, happened in Sarajevo itself. People were arrested like this, held in prisons, and killed, like his -- this witness's friend, Dr. Najdanovic. There was never any terror in the sense the indictment describes it, rather it existed in Sarajevo, literally speaking, and it was of the nature described by this witness. This is nothing other but terrorist behaviour. Of course it is up to you to determine the relevance of this, but the disappearing of people, detaining people, and keeping them in camps in the AOR of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that area is a textbook example of terror, as is interpreted by the entire world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but even if that is so, how does it become relevant to the charges of terror against the accused? Because even if we agree that it is terror, that would not mean that the Prosecution's allegation of terror against the accused is not substantiated. They may very well have been terrorised, the doctor and his friends, but what I am not seeing from your submission is an explanation as to how that helps you, assists the Defence, in relation to the Prosecution's charge of terror against the accused. That's what you need to explain to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have explained on several occasions, upon your request, was that the intensity of combat activity on the part of Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was something that needed response. What the Army of Republika Srpska did was not a campaign directed at civilians. What we were able to hear from witnesses, who like this witness were able to cross to the other side, as we will hear during the material time he managed to cross over, that means that what we managed to hear from those people about the things happening in the territory of Republika Srpska was something that strengthened their determination to preserve the positions they had, not to respond in the same way and they never did, we submit. But rather, this strengthened their decision and wish to hold on to their own, particularly during the time of command of Dragomir Milosevic. They wanted to keep their positions so as not to suffer the same fate as the people who were on the other side. Such things particularly did not happen in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps AOR during the time of command of Dragomir Milosevic. We've already explained this, and it is a very important reason that kept them at their positions. It only strengthened their determination, and they only undertook the activities that were necessary to do so. However, that did not amount to any sort of campaign on the part of the Army of Republika Srpska, particularly during the material time, that was directed against civilians. This encompasses June, July, and the following months. There was no such a campaign in place in particular between August 1994 and until 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll maintain my objection, underlining that we're here talking about a pre-indictment period. There might be some marginal issue of relevance if this was something that had occurred during the period of the indictment, but we're talking about a period sometime a year more ahead of the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's not an easy matter to determine the relevance of this evidence. It is not abundantly clear that it is -- that it is relevant. For one, it deals with the pre-indictment period, as Ms. Edgerton says. Are you going to be bringing evidence from this witness about the indictment period? Please don't make a speech. Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was about to move to that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And then some of my -- one of my colleagues is particularly concerned about the absence of any evidence relating to the specific incidents in the indictment, and has urged me to inquire whether you have any evidence in relation to those incidents, the incidents of sniping and shelling that are set out in the indictment. Or is that not part of the case that you are presenting to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, through this witness -- I have to go back yet again to the indictment. It is quite certain, and I have to repeat on this occasion as well, that the indictment probably would not have dealt itself with the time until August 1994, and had it not been so we would have had a much easier task. Sorry, I have to correct myself. Not the indictment, the Defence would like -- would have liked not to have to refer to the time preceding the time of command of Dragomir Milosevic, which is August 1994 until the 21st of November, 1995. In that case, Defence could have dealt with the situation on a far more easier way. However, I feel obliged to state yet again that a mere month before the beginning of the trial we received an amended indictment. There was no possibility to submit any procedural submission or objection to it. However, the changes were capital. It states that Dragomir Milosevic as of the day when he assumed command inherited the command and the campaign and pursued it further, as it existed until that time. Therefore, Defence was found in a situation in which it could not forego of a single day before the time in the indictment, concluding all the general matters that preceded it. Therefore, we felt obliged to tackle the events of 1992, 1993, and to introduce such witnesses as this one. This witness, this doctor, will also testify about certain things that Dr. Pejic had mentioned, which is the victims, the wounded, and casualties that he was able to observe while working in one hospital and then in another one. You approved of such testimony at that time after a written submission by the Prosecutor on the lack of relevance, and after our written submission and the discussion that followed, you decided still that it had relevance, since the victims on the other side did not exist in a vacuum. They speak to the intensity of activities of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly in the summer of 1995, whereas during an entire lengthy period of time preceding that one there were no such combat activities. This witness should complete his part of testimony in the next ten minutes concerning the initial phase, and then we wanted to move on to the other phase of his testimony, which is when he worked in the other hospital and he can tell us whom he treated there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what period does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The period of the summer of 1994 until the end of the war. Summer 1994 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think we'd be more interested in hearing that. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, it's not really a question, but this is an observation I'd like to make. As our Presiding Judge has said, the work we do is a very delicate job. There is equality of arms between the Prosecution and the Defence, and both parties need to submit their arguments. As far as I'm concerned, I understand full well the position of the Prosecutor and I understand -- or at least I tried to understand because the Prosecution has presented us with an indictment. And you wish to challenge this indictment. And this is why I'm making an effort and trying to understand what it is you're doing. I want to make sure that I understand what you are doing correctly. So we have the pre-indictment period and we have -- so we have the period which precedes the time when Dragomir Milosevic commanded the unit, and then we have the period which covers the time when Dragomir Milosevic was the commander. And you are right in saying that according to the indictment he inherited the campaign from General Galic. And this is -- your argument goes to the terror charge when you say this. And what I would like to know is whether the terror existed because it was due to Dragomir Milosevic or that it was a pervasive terror that was there anyway because of the various sides that were combatting each other. Now, for the period which starts at the time when Dragomir Milosevic was commanding the SRK, what I would like to know is this: Are you saying that terror did not exist or existed for all and everyone without any distinction, and whether you are going to dwell on the incidents which the Prosecution mentions in its indictment? You don't have to, of course, you have your own strategy, but this is just a question I want to put to you because I'd like to know. Once Dragomir Milosevic was a commander of the SRK, are you going to once again dwell on the issue of terror or are you going to rebut the arguments of the Prosecution relating more specifically to all the incidents contained in the indictment? This is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, had we stayed with the original indictment that was in force until a month before the trial began, I would have dealt exclusively with that time-period and I would have tried to demonstrate what the period from December to -- from August to December 1994 was like, and from December to May 1995 and onwards. However, what we were able to do in relation to certain incidents from the indictment, we did and we managed to gather the number of exhibits that were available relating to those incidents. During the time of the events, no officer of the Army of Republika Srpska was able to go across to the side under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to check for possible evidence relating to the period of command of Dragomir Milosevic. So what we are trying to show is that it was not possible to conduct any kind of research or investigation because it was absolutely out of the question to cross over to the other side and to establish certain things. What we can do in the context of the evidence presented by the Prosecutor is to deal with each of the incidents, but in order to analyse each of those incidents we need to wait till the end of the trial. And we will most definitely try to present our arguments to you, whereby we consider that the incidents were not proved as an act of direct fire by the accused, Dragomir Milosevic. And, Your Honour, Judge Mindua, that will be our most difficult and most important task. It will be our most important task, and we believe that based on the evidence already presented by the Prosecutor, we can point to certain things and show that the incidents that the indictment is based on are not the way the Prosecutor is presenting them. In some cases, such as in the case of a witness heard by you a few days ago here or there was a witness here who spoke about events relating to Grdonja we can discuss those documents but it is not possible for us to find witnesses from the actual place where things happened. But based on the evidence presented by the Prosecutor we can demonstrate that many of them were victims of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the Defence understands this to be as its most difficult task to deal with the incidents. However, in these circumstances all we can do now is to talk about the things that we can prove. First of all, that there was no such campaign. Absolutely there was no such campaign as something that dominated. This is the most serious part of the indictment. That there was no terrorising the population. But, as I explained several times before, I don't want to repeat it, what we are trying to show is that the campaign, that's the gist of the indictment, and then we intend to deal with the incidents. So we are obliged when the time comes to present to you all of our reasons in relation to each specific incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. Just one really important point to make of a general nature because Mr. Tapuskovic keeps repeating that the Prosecution changed kind of the rules of the game by issuing its new indictment, amended indictment, a month before trial. The indictment word by word almost verbatim followed the old indictment, and it just spelled it out more clearly. Because already in the old indictment in paragraph 4 it says: "For 44 months the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps implemented a military strategy which used shelling and sniping to kill, maim, wound, and terrorise the civilian inhabitants of Sarajevo. The shelling and sniping killed and wounded thousands of civilians of both sexes and all ages, including civilian children and the elderly." It goes on already in the original indictment to talk about the role of the accused as the Chief of Staff under General Galic. The word "inherited" is a new word which just spells out that the Chief of Staff during the Galic period took over this campaign outlined in the Galic indictment. It was more clear. It talks more about the, perhaps, the previous roles the accused had as a commander of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade in 1992, but the characteristics of the campaign did not change at all. So it's really important for me to tell you, Mr. President, Your Honours, that the case was exactly the same under the old indictment and under the new indictment. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But to the extent that you say that the accused inherited the campaign of General Galic, it would assist the Defence to show that there was no such campaign during General Galic's time for the accused to inherit. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, and they are totally free to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. Before I continue my examination-in-chief, and I don't have too much left, I'm going to finish before the break, I would like to tender the 65 ter document 3388 as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as D289, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T-61, perhaps we can cover things were quickly now. Let's not go back to the prison. How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was exchanged and crossed over to the Serb side on the 16th of June, 1994. I was imprisoned for five and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hospital was east of Sarajevo, some 3 kilometres to the east the airport on the slopes of Trebevic, close to Mojmilo hill. And soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska were mostly treated there as well as civilians from the Grbavica, Vrace, and the Ilidza area around Nedzarici and Trnovo and Kalinovik, and partially Trebevic, from all those settlements, Dobrinja and so on, Lukavica, as well as the other closer neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said you got there in June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Late June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, late June. Did you ever meet General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I saw him was here. I heard of his name, of course, but I don't know when he took over his position from the previous commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your job. What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly I was working in the hospital. I was sleeping there as well. I spent four months under the Treskavica in the place of Kalinovik where we had mobile medical units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in the hospital until after the war, until March or April 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, if you can just answer a few more questions. You got there in late June. Can you please describe the situation there until the end of 1994 in terms of the wounded. You said that you treated civilians and soldiers. Can you, please, describe that time until the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm no longer in private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall that period from the time that I arrived at the Kasindol Hospital until the end as a relatively peaceful period. There weren't many military actions. The number of soldiers was not that large. More wounded tended to come from Grbavica, because that was densely populated and it was close to a place we called Debelo Brdo or Debeli Brijeg which was behind the neighbourhood and there was fire from war weapons from that area. I believe one afternoon I treated four women who were seriously wounded. I guess there was more activity in terms of fire that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness T-61, how long did this quiet period last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was until sometime in October. Already in October we had to move the mobile surgical unit to Kalinovik and we had to take a detour of some 300 kilometres because the Kalinovik-Sarajevo or the Kalinovik-Kasindol road was cut for the wounded and we had to relocate the mobile surgical unit, numbering three surgeons and other staff to an institution in Kalinovik. We had to take a detour of some 300 kilometres in order to reach Kalinovik, even though it's 50 kilometres away if you took the usual route there. Activities intensified then but this was more in Treskavica in those areas of the -- not so much in the civilian neighbourhoods, and that's when we started to treat more soldiers and more civilian from Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long did this last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to determine the exact period, but we stayed up there throughout the winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did a different period follow that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the summer, if you're thinking of 1995 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm thinking of early 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in early 1995, it could have been March. Well let's say it was late March/early spring, there was activities on Igman and Treskavica and I was on Kasindol at the time while my other colleagues were in Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the period that you remember? What do you remember that was characteristic for that period, that is, out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in June or July 1995 and November 1995, I remembered in June I was in Kasindol and in November I was in Kalinovik. Kalinovik was intensely shelled. There was a pupil killed in front of her school at the time, and the facility we were in also was hit but there was no major damage. And I was hit by shrapnel, but it only got my trousers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in June and July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you thinking of 1995?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a very difficult period. I think that that was when Lukavica was bombed and the buildings around Kalinovik also. The bridges in Foca were bombed and the communications were cut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, I'm interested in the Sarajevo municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Sarajevo municipalities are Lukavica, which was intensely bombarded, it lost several buildings, a few civilians were hit, including some soldiers; and Trnovo also suffered a lot of damage. Since our team could not get through to Trnovo, we called a team from the Foca Hospital, which then went to Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many wounded were there at the time and what was the type of injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most injuries were caused by shelling because the sides were farther apart and plain gun fire was useless. If you mean in terms of structure, I can tell you that there were many more civilians who were wounded in Trnovo than soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I note the time, and in light of the fact that the greater part of this witness's testimony this morning dealt with events around Kosevo Hospital, the use of weapons, none of which we had received any notice of in the 65 ter summary, I wonder if I might make this unusual request, that we take the break now and resume at the normal time, which would give me a chance to review his earlier testimony in detail and finalise my cross-examination. I think it might work to expedite things later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have characterised it as an unusual request, Ms. Edgerton, but you have made it before. But it's still -- Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, it is stated clearly: [In French]" -- The beginning of the armed conflict in Sarajevo and the activities from the Kosevo Hospital." [In B/C/S] It is very clearly stated -- it is clearly stated in the summary that we were to deal with the activities from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, in all the circumstances we will grant the request. We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness 61, and that's how I'll refer to you, I'd like to ask you some questions today based on some of the testimony you've given and some of the things you've said previously to this Tribunal and to other authorities. Now, if you can't understand anything that I say, if it's not clear or if you don't hear it, you'll please tell me, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to clear up a couple of things. From what I understand from you, from January to June 1994, you were detained. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the 2nd of January and the 16th of June that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from your exchange, if I can call it that, until the end of the conflict you were not within Bosnian-held territory in any regard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you have no information then based on personal experience as to the situation within Sarajevo from January 1994. That's when your personal experience ended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that there was no personal experience, but I watched television and listened to the radio on -- from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "from both sides," by that I take to mean you listened to Serb radio and TV as well as Bosnian radio and TV. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you put it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, am I also correct when I say that I understand that during the conflict there were actually at least three hospitals in Bosnian-held Sarajevo that received patients, the Kosevo Hospital, the state hospital, and the hospital in Dobrinja. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The Dobrinja Hospital was a small facility of some 20 beds in total. It was headed by Hadzi Jusuf who used to be my work mate. I used to be his boss.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, people then came to these hospitals for help actually depending on the area in which they were or maybe their ability to access the hospital safely. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, it was a bit different, but later it was as you put it. The first five or six months of the war there was a distribution centre of sorts in place. It was housed in the clinic where I worked, and the distribution was done by the team that I headed. We were but one of the surgical clinics. We also sent people to the state hospital, which used to be the military hospital. We did not send people to the Dobrinja facility, though, because access to it was difficult. It was risky to go there and it was also small.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another area. You, I understand then, personally didn't see whether from August 1994 to November 1995 there were armed soldiers in or around Kosevo Hospital; it was simply impossible, you weren't there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct, and I wasn't able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Similarly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: However, I have to add something. One could see the civil engineering faculty close to the hospital on television. One could see the exercises conducted there by different troops. Therefore, we did have some indirect information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll get to the subject of the media towards the end, actually, of our time together. But just to go on along this line, similarly, you personally did not see whether between August 1994 and November 1995 Bosnian forces fired anything from the hospital ground or the facilities? You weren't there, you didn't see it. Anything you learned from the media was second-hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was 10 kilometres away. I wasn't able to see that -- or maybe 12 or 15 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In line -- that is, page 34, line 9, there was a mention of artillery exercises, whereas it says here "troops." It doesn't reflect accurately what the witness had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you say the witness actually said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague followed the transcript. There was a mention of an artillery school that trained there. Perhaps the witness can confirm or correct us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, that wasn't the question I had asked initially, and I don't quite follow the issue with respect to the transcript any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but let us just have the witness tell us. What is it that you said, Witness, about seeing either troops or exercises conducted there by different troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was in Sarajevo until the 3rd of January, 1994, that is, there was an artillery school there which was founded in the first couple of months of the war. I believe it remained there until the end of the war, but I cannot know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understood -- my question went to whether or not the witness had seen Bosnian forces firing anything from the hospital ground between August 1994 and November 1995, and I'll leave it, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm interested to find out from the witness. The artillery school of which you speak was established by whom? And exactly where was it located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The school was in the building of the faculty of civil engineering and of architecture. It is one building with two wings. My older daughter used to study architecture in that building. I went there once in the summer of 1992 to pick up her documents. They wouldn't let me in, however. There was a guard posted there and the artillery school had already been established. The lady who was in charge of the student office was escorted into the building. She was allowed to go, but I was not. When going to work and passing by the building every day, I could see both troops and guards there, of course while I was in Sarajevo, in the part of it that was under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So exactly where was it located in relation to the hospital? Was it actually in the hospital or beside it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't in the hospital. It was 50 or 70 metres below the building I worked in. There were four buildings in total. One was the faculty, one was the traffic institute, one was the institute for testing construction material, and this last building was some 20 metres away from the building where I worked. And the rest was within the perimeter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And this was established by the ABiH, the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of BiH, there was no other army there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, the Prosecution is prepared to concede that sometime in June or July 1992 there were two tanks initially stored at the Faculty of Engineering and Architecture grounds, which are about a hundred metres from the Kosevo Hospital complex. That's the concession we're prepared to make. However, very quickly one was rendered inoperable and the other was moved to Ciglane tunnel. This is one of the points we raised in the adjudicated facts that was ruled upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But do you concede that an artillery school was established there?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, my learned friend said that they are ready to concede. It is a type of testimony. I would expect the Prosecutor to ask the witness: How many pieces were there. The learned friend said: We concede, we are ready to accept, and we haven't heard anything concerning that from the witness. I believe I have to object to that. The witness did not provide any answers to my learned friend's question about tanks, whereas she said: We are ready to accept that there were two tanks. I think it is an open-ended question and out of place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, maybe I'm not understanding Ms. Edgerton. Ms. Edgerton, as I understand it, has not put any questions to the witness. Have you put questions to the witness about the existence of tanks?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was specifically limited to 1994/1995 period, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- but in light of the discussion that was going on between Your Honour and my friend, I was prepared to make this concession on behalf of the Prosecutor which might clarify matters and expedite matters somewhat, especially since we're dealing with a pre-indictment period by two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the concession is in relation to 1992. And being a concession, I mean, she doesn't have to put questions to the witness about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, I mean, it's a matter for you to decide how you react to it, Mr. Tapuskovic, how you react to the concession.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I move on, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness 61, just to get back on track, you personally -- and this is going to involve a bit of repetition. You personally didn't see whether, between August 1994 and November 1995, there were armed soldiers in or around Kosevo Hospital. Is that correct? You personally didn't see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the third time, I was unable to see that. I was 12 kilometres away at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And that -- the same goes for whether Bosnian forces fired anything from hospital grounds or facilities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the same goes for whether there were any tanks or other heavy weapons located in the area of the hospital compound. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was all close to the hospital grounds. Let us not mix two different things. The tanks were very close to the perimeter of the hospital, as I've been saying. But as to what was happening from January 1994 until 1995 and on to the end of the war, I don't know, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the same goes for whether or not there were actually any operational military facilities in or around the hospital. And maybe for the sake of clarity we could talk about the Kosevo Hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you're referring to the period from 1994 onwards, I don't know that. But the school I mentioned which was in the immediate vicinity of the hospital remained there until the end of the war, because the faculty of architecture was located in the medical school and another faculty in the School of Mechanical Engineering throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But is my understanding -- your assertion to that effect is based entirely on second-hand knowledge, what you might have seen through the media. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, because I watched both television programmes, the Serbian and the Bosnian, and also I received some newspapers from UNPROFOR soldiers. I'm referring to newspapers from the Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, because you simply weren't there, you can't say anything about the frequency of admissions of patients to Kosevo Hospital with shelling or sniping injuries during this August 1994 to November 1995 period, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no answer to that question. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Going back to the period of time that you were there, sir, you mentioned in your evidence in chief about the proportion of civilian wounded to the proportion of wounded people who might have been engaged in military activity. Am I correct if I say that that proportion could actually vary from hospital to hospital because of the very different areas of the town they were located? Did you not hear what I said, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know from the information I had, I'm talking about the hospital in Nedzarici and Dobrinja, I wasn't there but it was mostly soldiers who were admitted there because the separation line was close. As for Kosevo Hospital, about 70 to 80 per cent were soldiers and the remainder was civilians. That is, of course, an average. There were days when the situation was different.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, sir, in your testimony earlier today you said 50 -- with regard to your hospital, you said 50 to 60 per cent of the wounded were soldiers and 30 to 40 per cent civilians. Are you now saying that the proportion that you had earlier set out is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, 15 years have elapsed and it's difficult to be precise about percentages. This is just an impression. Nobody kept track of this and wrote reports about it, so it's hard to answer such a question. Was it 3 or 5 per cent more or less? Well, it's impossible to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, though, would you -- all right. Would you be able to say this: Were shelling and sniping incidents, although the numbers varied, constant until the time you were arrested? Were the -- let me rephrase it to be clearer. Were -- did you see injuries caused as a result of shelling or sniping throughout the time you were there until you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that, although it's hard to tell what a sniper wound is actually, because you can always tell whether somebody was wounded by artillery or by shrapnel, but whether it was a sniper or not, you can't say. And a person can actually have a chance of surviving and getting to the surgeon if the sniper has made a mistake and not hit the target. Snipers mostly aim at the head and the chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What proportion --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of the [Realtime transcript read in error "other than"] civilians, were the greater proportion injured by sniping? Of the civilians. The transcript reads "other than civilians". Of the civilians, were the greater proportion injured by sniping, as opposed to military -- as opposed to any other injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Explain to you, Madam, that a surgeon can never distinguish between a sniper wound and other wounds. They can distinguish between wounds caused by an explosive device and wounds caused by artillery weapons. So we had explosive wounds and entry wounds. That was what we saw as surgeons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you include -- when you say an "entry wound," are you using that to describe a gun-shot wound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both. An explosive device can also have an entry wound or an entry/exit wound, but they look different.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They must look vastly different, don't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What proportion of the civilian patients you treated were injured by explosive wounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's hard for me to be precise as to the percentages after a lapse of 15 to 17 years, but perhaps after a half were gun-shot wounds and about a half were explosive wounds. However, one has to understand that it was different on different days. When there was fighting, many people arrived in civilian clothes and said they were civilians, but some of them were actually soldiers in civilian clothing. So it was very hard to distinguish and no precise statistics were ever kept, let alone published.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, with respect, in Sarajevo during the conflict there were really two types of injuries, weren't there, those caused by explosives and those caused by shooting. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've already said that twice today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And all of the civilians that you treated with rare exception came to your clinic victims of those kinds of injuries. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had both kinds of wounds if you're talking about the kinds of weapons that were used.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You actually -- you've treated civilians for injuries as a result of shelling and sniping from as early as April 1992, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the third time there is reference to sniping. The witness explained more than once that there were gun-shot wounds and explosive wounds, and those could be distinguished. My learned friend keeps referring to sniping, but the witness said quite decidedly that he could only establish whether the wound was a gun-shot or an explosive wound. For the third time my learned friend is referring to sniping, although the witness explained that he could not tell the difference between sniping and other kinds of gun-shot wounds. He could only distinguish between gun-shot wounds and explosive wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's true, Ms. Edgerton. The witness has said time and again that he can't distinguish sniping from shelling wound. So it's not fair to put to him a question that he has treated civilians for injuries as a result of shelling and sniping.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He doesn't accept -- he has not been able to make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He did say, Your Honour, with respect that gun-shot wounds and explosive wounds were vastly different. I think the distinction is between sniping as opposed to any other kind of small-arms fire. So perhaps I could use the word small-arms fire, injuries from small-arms fire. Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could go back to the question, my original question, sir, you've treated injuries as a result of small-arms fire and shelling from as early as April 1992, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Madam, but I have to explain that a hand-grenade is also a fire weapon, but there are only two kinds of war wounds. I am a specialist in war wounds, that's my specialty. A surgeon can distinguish only between a wound caused by a bullet and a wound caused by an explosion, a shell, a hand-grenade, and so on. No other distinctions can be made by a surgeon. Any other distinction made by a surgeon would be medically untenable.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Hand-grenades are also weapons carried by infantry soldiers. Each one has several hand-grenades with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have a document brought up on the screen for the witness, please, 03381. I'm sorry, the B/C/S version of the document maybe could be made a tiny bit smaller.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, can you see the document on the right-hand side of the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Am I correct when I say this is a medical report on a --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, I knew this doctor. He was killed, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a medical report on a woman hit by a shell, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. It was a piece of shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On April 5th of 1992. Doesn't, sir, the presence or the notation that shrapnel is recovered from the injury denote an injury caused by a mortar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An explosive device, we don't know whether it was a mortar, a bomb, a rocket, or something else, but it was certainly an explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. We seem to be missing a second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe I should turn my microphone on. Thank you. Could we not broadcast this second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, under -- on this page 2 that appears in front of you under the heading "Case History," which says -- do you not see where it says that this woman was hit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you not see where it says that this woman was hit by a shell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I said that even before I saw this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does that document appear to you to be authentic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could have that entered as a Prosecution exhibit, please, and it should probably be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why should that be so? Why, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In my confusion over what I thought was a missing second page of the document, I forgot to ask the witness a question with respect to the second page. Let me try again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll need a redaction and I'll withdraw the document. Mystery solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have 03383, please. Does this document have a second page? This document should also not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is also signed, but there is no indication it was signed by this doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We need another redaction, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Another redaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'll withdraw the document and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony in the Galic case and today and in your statement that you gave to RS authorities some years ago, you said that you had seen shells falling on the Kosevo Hospital on many occasions in the period 1992 to 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw three shells landing. I was at the clinic when two of them landed, and the third landed in the upper right-hand corner of the clinic while I was away, but I saw the hole it made.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you were actually in the hospital when three shells landed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there when two shells landed. The third fell while I was absent, but I saw the place where it landed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying that between the whole period of 1992 and 1994, the Kosevo Hospital was shelled on only three occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the traumatology ward, where I was working. The Kosevo Hospital is a large complex of buildings, but we heard shells landing nearby. And I'm certain that about ten shells landed on the Kosevo Hospital. I know one fell on the eye clinic which is outside the compound; one on the orthopaedic clinic; and two or three --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear which clinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you just repeat what you said, Doctor. And two or three, the interpreter didn't get the last part of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was present at the traumatology ward when two shells landed there. Fortunately one of them did not go off, it didn't explode. And a third fell on the traumatological ward while I was absent, but I saw the place where it landed. Another one landed on the orthopaedic clinic which I saw for myself, not the shell falling but the place where it fell. And I heard that one landed in the corridor of the eye clinic but that was outside the Kosevo compound, and on that occasion a friend of mine, Dr. Vladimir Deljanik was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How big is the Kosevo compound, sir, how many hectares of territory does it cover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just list the buildings. It's a complex of 12 to 14 buildings, and it covers quite a large area but I can't tell you how many square metres it covers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 12 to 14 different clinics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was also an administrative building, there was a special building for the boiler room in the technical services, and the remainder were clinics.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, he said 12 to 14 buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not 12 to 14 clinics.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about Kosevo Hospital being hit. Would you agree with me that you're of the understanding that it was Serb forces, in particular the SRK, firing at Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's correct that the Serb forces were firing on the Kosevo Hospital, but I know because my office at the clinic faced the faculty of building construction, which I mentioned, and there were always two, three, or four firings in the direction of Poljine where the Serb forces were and then there was a response. I cannot say that the shell which landed on the orthopaedic clinic was from that area because it was not accessible from Poljine. So the shell must have come from some other direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- when shelling started from the technical faculty or the building construction faculty, we always took shelter in the upper part of the building, which was a bit further away and which was safer. And we would take the patients further away from that side facing the technical faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, I understand your testimony that you found -- you feel that shelling of your clinic on at least two occasions may have been a response to fire from the Bosnian forces. But are you asserting that all the shelling on the Kosevo Hospital compound was responsive to fire from the Bosnian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't assert that about the time when I wasn't there, when I was at home. But it was like that when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What about the shell that fell on the orthopaedic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just want to have that clarified. So, Doctor, you're saying that when you were at the hospital all the firing from the RSK forces was responsive, responsive, that is, to firing from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say about every firing because I wasn't at the hospital all the time, but the two shells that landed while I was at the clinic were responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you indicated that those were responsive to fire from what you described as small tanks. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First there was fire from small tanks, they were smaller in size; and then about ten minutes, after two or three firings were made, there would be a response towards the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that response was with mortars as well as artillery, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, mortars are also artillery. Everything that fires explosive devices is artillery. We don't know what was used. We only know that there were shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
