utterances.text: Would you agree that the shells were designed -- the shells used against the hospital were designed not to eliminate tanks but to inflict as much damage as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what use it would be for them to inflict damage on patients who were not able to fight. They were firing at the tanks that were close to the hospital, but because the hospital compound was close by and in view of the distance involved, very small error would result in a projectile landing on the hospital. Well, patients are irrelevant as targets for an army since they are not able to fight. And it's not worth wasting weapons, wasting ammunition, for any army on people like that, on patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you would disagree when I would put to you that the fire that was returned on the hospital was actually designed to inflict -- to kill, actually, and injure as many people as possible? It was, sir, in fact, a completely inappropriate weapon to return fire on a tank with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're not right. The fire was to silence the tank weapons around the hospital, but since the place from where it was fired was quite away, then a small mistake in targeting made the shells drop around the hospital. If you are talking about shelling in general, the hospital would not be very difficult to hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, sir, you've just said two times now: A small mistake in targeting resulted in the hospital being hit. Doesn't that speak volumes to you about the inappropriateness of that kind of -- the use of that kind of weapon against a hospital facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps the intention was not for that to be used against the hospital facilities. It was intended to destroy the tanks that were below the hospital. It would have been very easy to hit the hospital, and any weapon could be able to hit the buildings in the hospital complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness. Do you recall whether the tanks were still present by the time the two shells were fired back? In other words, had the two tanks that had fired the shots against Poljine, were they still in the vicinity when the fire was returned or had they already left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The tanks were there throughout the time that I was at the hospital until the 1st of January, 1994. They were always around the faculty buildings. They moved around, they fired shells, and then would move out of the way quickly. But for as long as I was there, they were constantly in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you are saying that the tanks who fired the shots which triggered the response from the RSK remained in the same position by the time the fire was returned. They did not move around or away; that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, perhaps we didn't understand each other or it was misinterpreted. The tanks were camouflaged. They moved around in that area and they were always in that area. They would just move around a little bit, as much as they could. It's quite a large compound. There are large trees. It was like a large park where the faculty buildings were, and the tanks stayed there throughout that whole time. Of course they would move back 50, 100, 150 metres back or forward. They would shield themselves behind buildings or behind the institute for the -- for construction materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, sir, if they move out of the way quickly after they fired 50, 100, or 150 metres, why then launch return fire with something like a mortar, which is designed to injure as many people as possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness did not say "mortars." Once he said that he was not able to establish what weapons were used for firing. He never mentioned mortars. He was very certain when he said that he could not know which weapons were involved, but the Prosecutor is insisting on something that the witness did not actually mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also I doubt very much whether he can say why fire was returned with something like a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, do you find, having been there at the time, did you find the type of weapon that you saw used against the hospital to have been an appropriate weapon in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, on the witness's behalf, you would have to explain what you mean by "appropriate," Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would a weapon of the type you saw used against the hospital, with the damage it must have caused, in your mind have been an appropriate weapon to use against a medical complex?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer the question yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness does not have to answer this question. He's not in a position to give that kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, you actually have no way of knowing what the intention of the SRK gunners were, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness's microphone needs to be switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the intentions, but the fact is that shells did drop only around the edges of the hospitals or at the buildings that were facing the faculty of engineering. And I think the ear, nose, and throat clinic was hit once, that building. The other buildings were not hit. So it was our impression that the hospital was not deliberately targeted, and the shells that did hit the hospital in our view were due to imprecision in targeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you tell us roughly the distance between Poljine and the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never went to Poljine, but I estimate that it's 3 to 4 kilometres as the crow flies. But I was never at Poljine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, just going back to your answer for His Honour Judge Robinson, you said: "So it was our impression that the hospital was not deliberately targeted." Are you saying, sir, that the hospital -- are you describing your impression throughout the period up until the date of your arrest or only with respect to those two occasions you've given evidence about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It refers to the whole period, because as I said before in answer to a previous question, the hospital complex is large. It has 13 or 14 buildings. So if anybody was deliberately targeting the hospital, they could not fail to hit something. The hits, as I mentioned, were on the parts of the building that were facing the faculty complex.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, first of all, sir, I thought that you had said earlier on in your testimony that you couldn't give evidence with respect to -- no, sorry, let me withdraw that. So your assertion is that from 1992 to 1994 Kosevo Hospital was not deliberately targeted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my assertion and that is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us -- you must tell us why. Tell us why you have come to that conclusion, that it wasn't deliberately targeted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's easy to get to a conclusion. The hospital is a large complex of 12 to 14 buildings. Whoever wanted to fire at the hospital would hit any of the buildings. All the hits during the time that I was there were on buildings that were facing the civil engineering faculty, and that is why we understood that to be missed targeting or a mistake and not a deliberate targeting of the hospital. No shell hit the clinic for infectious diseases, for skin diseases, or internal medicines or the surgery clinic, all the clinics that were inside of the complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I've understood you correctly, the shells did not hit the hospital which, according to you, was fairly easy to hit. Do you know whether shells might have hit the tanks that were around the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that they did, but if they didn't actually fire at them at least they could have prevented them from moving around in the compound and from firing there. Of course they are much more difficult to hit than a building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you be prepared to agree, Witness, that there was a substantial risk in trying to return fire to eliminate those tanks, given their location as you've testified, a risk of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fortunately, when I was there there were no civilian casualties at the hospital, but that there was a certain risk, yes, that is true. I cannot estimate the level of the risk because that would depend on the persons who were firing and the extent of their experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What buildings faced the civil engineering faculty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat that for the third time. It was the traumatology clinic, that was the first and the closest; then it was the building of the ear, nose, and throat clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And these were all buildings that faced in the direction north, towards Poljine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were facing the civil engineering building, but they were turned towards Poljine on their -- the side of the building, the facing -- the face -- the front of the building faced the civil engineering faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What about those portions of the compound, those buildings within the compound, that faced the area of Trebevic, the opposite area? Were they not targeted and hit between 1992 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trebevic is quite far, and as far as I know the side facing Trebevic was hit only by one shell which hit the orthopaedic clinic. There were no other shells that could have come from that direction towards Kosevo, not when I was there at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, during the period of time you were at Kosevo Hospital, did you have electricity throughout?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. There was electricity intermittently. Sometimes we used the generators and sometime we didn't have either.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you have running water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At times the water was cut.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you have sufficient medical supplies to meet your needs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can never have enough medical equipment in wartime, especially surgical equipment. We had certain stocks made before the war, and then the humanitarian started to arrive. So we did have enough, but it was barely enough. We made some of it ourselves. I myself made a device to immobilise bones from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did any staff member, any of your colleagues from 1992, 1994 -- to 1994 manifest any emotional effects of living and working under shelling and gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the personal effects were because of those factors, but I know that the Serb staff that worked there was abused. They were called Chetniks --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That wasn't my question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- But it was mostly done by the citizens and the soldiers, not by the medical staff. Can you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute. She mentioned his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, yes. A redaction, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I've set a record today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I could repeat my question, Witness. Did any staff member manifest, over the course of the two years you remained on duty, any emotional effects of living and working under shelling and gun-fire? My question is specific to the conditions at the time caused by shelling and gun-fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had contacts with the staff at the traumatology clinic as well as with my team of 12 to 16 surgeons and some 30 other medical staff. There were no such effects amongst them. As for the other part of the medical centre that employed between 15 to 1600 staff, I really would not know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you heard no one complain of being tired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everyone was tired.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You heard no one complain of being cold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the winter I was cold as well as the others. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You heard no one complain of being hungry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There wasn't that much food, but there was always something. There wasn't that much of a choice, but there was always something to eat and it was distributed to the staff that worked at the clinic. Sometimes I spent ten days there without going home, and I must say that each day I received two meals and they were not very big and they were quite modest, but they were meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You heard no one complain of being depressed from having to come to work, for example, tired, cold, or hungry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if they were depressed, but I know that most people were scared.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "most people," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the medical staff and the wounded and the patients who came to the hospital. These were the people that I had contacts with.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you hear anybody complain of difficulties they had making their way to and from work in the day because of shelling or gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were such cases. I cannot tell you the frequency of that, and I don't know about all the people who worked at the Kosevo clinic. But I know that there were such cases amongst the people that I worked with, the people in my team.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you hear people complain because they had lost a friend or a member of their family or a neighbour over the course of the recent past to shelling or gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were such people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then what do you think they were scared of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They lived in a town that was in war. There is no person in war who does not believe that they could be wounded, killed. There is no war, especially in the hilly terrain where Sarajevo was, where there were no difficulties with heating and food. Of course I lived through two wars and I have personal experience how that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Those are my questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have just a few questions along the same vein as the questions put by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While -- when you moved to work at the hospital, Witness T-61, on the other side- how shall I put it? - and now you spent time there from the summer of 1994 until the end of the conflict. Now, I would ask you, these hospitals, and then when you were out in the field as well, did they always have sufficient electricity, water, medical equipment?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was electricity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- With respect, that doesn't arise from my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, does it arise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that is precisely what we are doing here the entire time. In response to my learned friend's questions, the witness explained. He spoke about the emotional stress, lack of food, and I'm just continuing and asking the same thing. And that is when he worked in this other hospital weren't the same problems prevalent there relating to food, fear of the war, psychological problems, and difficulties to actually reach your place of work, to get to work. And this does arise from questions put by my learned friend. I didn't ask these questions in my examination-in-chief. My colleague put the questions, and this arises directly from her questions. And I'm trying to see if it's possible that only one side suffered in the sense that my learned friend put the questions and got the answers to that or if the same situation in the experience of the witness was valid on the other side. And I'm just asking him whether the same conditions prevailed on the other side. Perhaps he can say that this wasn't so, that there was no fear, no suffering, there was always electricity, cake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Tapuskovic, but do it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. You have heard what this is all about. So I'm asking you: Is everything you said, that people suffered because there was a war on, if you can just say very briefly what this looked like. Because you were a person treating people on both sides at approximately the same time. So if you can say very briefly, I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, on the Serb side there were better food supplies, somewhat better. As for energy, it was the same. As for heating oil, it was a bit harder on the Serb side. As for medical equipment, it was much worse on the Serb side because that hospital was established at the beginning of the war and it had no stocks of supplies and humanitarian aid was distributed very unevenly, to the detriment of the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what you said about emotional stress and fear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was no difference. There was a separation line. There were troops on both sides, people were killed on both sides equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We are grateful to you for coming to the Tribunal to testify. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can call him straight away, but is it time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have five, six minutes, so we'll start.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness is Witness T-27, Borislav Kovacevic, who has no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as you know, I am the Defence counsel appearing for Dragomir Milosevic. We've already met and spoken. But first I would like you to tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Borislav Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were born on the 11th of May, 1963?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Ilijas, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed primary school in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Secondary school of electrical engineering in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the beginning of the conflict, you were employed in a company called Zrak and the plant you worked at was in Cevljanovici in Srednje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of that company was in Sarajevo in Buca Potok. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours something about the plant in Cevljanovici Srednje that belonged to the Zrak enterprise, what did it produce up to the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was a plant belonging to the Sarajevo Zrak company, and we worked on cutting glass for various companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the conflict began, did this plant continue operating?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. Every day we received material from the headquarters, from Zrak in Sarajevo. When the conflict broke out, the material stopped arriving so we were unable to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, should I continue or are we going to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At 20 past.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Witness, in order to save time, were you a member of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps starting from the first day of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was your role in that conflict?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the time, I was a fighter at the front line in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did you belong to at the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict, I was a member of the Ilijas Brigade until November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Ilijas Brigade up to that time you mentioned, November 1994?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: His name was Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The battalion commander was first Luka Vukovic, who was killed; and then there was Zeljko Micic, and he was also killed; and afterwards it was Acim Vukovic, Luka's brother, until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us up to what time you were a member of the Ilijas Brigade. Can you tell us again, and then what brigade did you become a member of after that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I was in the Ilijas Brigade until November 1994, and then as of November 1994 I was part of the 1st Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you said that you were in the 2nd Brigade. You told us which one it was, and who was the commander, what did you say?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The commander of that brigade was Vlado Lizdek.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The battalion commander was Dragan Pajic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a small clarification and I can do this in cross-examination, but I understand that the brigade had more than one battalion. So is the witness answering with respect to the battalion he was part of or which battalion in particular, if that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what particular battalion are you speaking of, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st Battalion of the 1st Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for not putting the question myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time Dragan Tupajic, the commander of that 1st Battalion, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think he was about 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was he an officer?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. He worked on civilian protection. We didn't have any real officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you didn't have any real officers, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I mean we didn't have trained officers who had been officers in the JNA. It was simply up to us to be both soldiers, privates, and officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that 1st Battalion of yours, what kind of people were in it, where they were from?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They were local people, the inhabitants of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours as you said that from the beginning of the conflict you were a fighter of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Do you remember initially what weapons were there -- first of all, tell us what kind of weapons you, yourself, had because you said you were constantly in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We privates had only personal weapons, semi-automatic and automatic rifles. We also had some artillery, a few mortars and howitzers, and I used to see one tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps when, or rather, when Dragomir Milosevic was appointed commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry again, but the witness has given evidence that he was part of two brigades. And when my friend has asked him about the weapons he had is he referring to, because this was in response to a question of being a fighter of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, is he speaking of weapons in the Ilijas Brigade or in the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you speaking of, Witness, the Ilijas Brigade or the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman asked me about the beginning of the war, what kind of weapons we had then. At the beginning of the war until 1994, I was in the Ilijas Brigade. So now I'm referring to the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you now to explain this. I think my learned friend was a little bit hasty in his intervention. I'm asking you when General Dragomir Milosevic became the commander, regardless of which brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I'm asking you when he became the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the area where I was, in the trench, my combat area, there was quite a lot of activity. I think it was early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first tell me when this was.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in early August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, what brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were you in at the time of his arrival?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was in the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were transferred to the 1st Romanija Brigade, when did you say?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened immediately before General Dragomir Milosevic took over command -- but before that, let me ask you the following. I think I should ask you this first. You told us what the situation was with heavy weapons at the beginning of the conflict. What happened with reference to those weapons in 1994, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the first half of 1994, we were strengthened, we were reinforced, replenished with heavy weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm asking you -- oh, all right. I won't interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In the first half of 1994, we received more heavy weapons which arrived from Sarajevo in the -- from the part under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then explain what happened to those heavy weapons in 1994.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, starting in March I think, heavy weapons began to be withdrawn from the part of Sarajevo under our control. So in the Nisic plateau a lot of these weapons arrived. I saw about five tanks, quite a lot of artillery, and I heard from my comrades that a part of those weapons were sent off to Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now tell me, just before General Dragomir Milosevic took over command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did something happen in late August/early September but before his arrival?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was actually at the end of July. Throughout July there were attacks on our positions on the Nisici plateau and there was an offensive on the villages of the Vares municipality which gravitated towards Ilijas. In that offensive every day one of our villages fell. We didn't have enough fighters. My brother-in-law was killed, my sister was left a widow with two small children, he was buried there. But on the 2nd of August all the other villages fell, his grave was there, and with the help of this strengthened artillery and because we were motivated, we stopped the attacks on the Nisici plateau, and that was about that time that the general was appointed corps commander. During that fighting my town, Ilijas, was shelled night and day. There were many casualties. I have to mention two victims, I don't want to miss that. The first was a 6-year-old boy, his father was called Boban and his mother Andjelina the last name was Antunovic and a 14-year-old girl, the daughter of friends of mine Zdravko and Miloj Kabudrov [phoen]. There were other casualties but I feel I have to mention those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After General Milosevic's arrival, did the situation stabilise?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in mid-August, the situation stabilised. We strengthened our positions, and the fighters whose villages had previously fallen, they stayed with us at Vares with a certain amount of artillery. We managed to stop those attacks, and for a while things were quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any refugees who came to your area?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we took them in and directed them towards Vogosca and Ilijas. There were many wounded who were then forwarded to Pale and Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the months that followed, what was the situation like after mid-August?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In the second half of August and in September and October, things were quite calm. There were no significant operations underway. However, in end October and early November, there was a new attack on our positions. It was terrible. There were many soldiers of theirs there and artillery, many casualties on our side. Pedjo Arsic was killed then, also Vladimir Sepur [phoen], Slavisa Kosarac was seriously injured. There were many wounded and killed, but we managed to stop those attacks although they attacked non-stop for 10 to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you get any information about any movements of the 1st Corps of the ABiH? Did you have any information on that in October and November 1994?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our observers informed us that they were regrouping and that there were many, and such attacks were actually expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know where they were coming from?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We were told by the people from Ilidza and Sarajevo that many fighters left Sarajevo through the tunnel, and it was expected that they would be included in the very attacks on my positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was an agreement reached at a certain point between the belligerent parties and when?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had the media at our disposal and our command informed us about it in December 1994, they said there was an agreement in place, a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours how long was the agreement in place, at least at your positions?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The whole winter of 1994 and 1995, until spring. All the way until early June actually, things were quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in June?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In early June 1995, again we were informed by our superior command that strong enemy forces were regrouping and that a number of them left Sarajevo. An attack was expected. We sort of relaxed for the past five months or so, and we were also hoping for a lasting cease-fire. However, on the 15th of June, 1995, early in the morning, a lightning struck us. ABiH forces with strengthened artillery attacked against all positions at the Nisici plateau. We were a bit taken aback and suffered great losses. They managed to take over control of the Semizovac-Srednje road which was the only road to communicate with Ilijas and no ambulance could pass through to Sokolac. People were dying in the field. However, our morale was high and with a lot of artillery support we managed to regain that territory the very same day in the afternoon. We returned to the trenches and regained control of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were struck as if by a lightning and that there were severe actions and operations. What did you have in mind in particular? What did they use?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, they had a lot of personnel. The war has been ongoing for four years by that time, but all of a sudden there were ten to one. There was a lot of shelling as well. Many shells landed on the front lines but also overshot, landing in the rear on civilians. On the 16th they attacked again, even stronger since I guess they became frustrated because they lost the road which they managed to gain control of at a certain point. Many people died like the Djurovic family, Goran Rajic, someone named Ladanac [phoen] was severely injured as well as Luka Rajnic [phoen], many, many people, many names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the directions they attacked on the 15th and the 16th, and you mentioned the Semizovac-Srednje road, besides military losses were there any other casualties, particularly civilian?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to mention that. On the 16th the attacks were stronger and the shells cut off our telephone communication lines. There was no briefing that day, and we couldn't move anywhere from our trenches. Behind our backs there were our parents and our children. We simply could not leave. We had to defend them. On the 17th we were told that in Srednje, in my village, three people were killed between the 16th and the 17th. They were buried there. One of them was an ambulance driver, then Sejanovic Caca [phoen] and Nedeljko Rasovic, both elderly. Many, many victims, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There's no reason for me to ask many more questions. I just wanted to show you two documents. One was shown by another witness who came from the same area, it is DD002840. It is D282. Witness, have a look at the document. The things you said about the Srednje-Semizovac line and the events you mentioned, does that tally to what is mentioned in the document? Does it correspond to the events of those days? I had already shown this document to another witness. Please look at the heading, the date, and the second paragraph. Please read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, BH Army, 1st Corps command, forward command post - Igman. "Military secret strictly confidential 01/1-222, Igman, 15 June, 1995, time: 1400 hours. "Report: To the command" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "To," interpreter's correction, "The 3rd Corps forces with their 126th Brigade and the 134th Mountain Brigades, the 16th Battalion liberated on their axis of attack, the whole feature of Ravni Nabozic and Lipa, that is elevation 701, placing the Srednje-Semizovac communication and the Semizovac intersection under their full control."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which corps joined the 1st corps, the 16th Division, as stated?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It says here it was the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does it have anything to do with the fact you mentioned, which was that there were many more pieces they used in their attacks and that you were outnumbered ten to one? Is that -- was the situation like the one described in the document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly the thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to show the witness another document which has to do with certain events in the fall of 1994. I omitted that a few minutes ago, and I will thus conclude my examination. The document is DD --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. I saw Mr. Sachdeva rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's fine for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. I think you were about to do something in relation to a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an intervention from the accused, but however this document already has been admitted as D282.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The second document DD002466, Witness, a few moments ago you described the activities in 1994. I wanted to show you this document. Can you tell me whether it corresponds to the things happening in the field in the fall of 1994. As you can see here, what is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Supreme Command staff of the armed forces, command post Kakanj, strictly confidential "--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "02-1/1381-1, Kakanj, 7 November 1994." That's it. "Request and suggestion for organising" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us cut things short. Look at item 1, please. There are some locations mentioned. Please read those to yourself and tell us whether the activities you mentioned a little while ago when asked about the events of the fall of 1994, do these locations have anything to do with such combat activities?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the very locations at the Nisici plateau, the hills of Jasen and Polom, that's where the operations were and this is where the people I mentioned were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please read the document to the end, starting with: "Analysing ..." To the end.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: "Analysing your success and the enemy's current situation, I propose that you carry out a regrouping of forces and equipment in order to carry out the final attacks for the liberation of the Nisici plateau on the following axes: "Donji Potok - Gornji Ivancici; Stomorine - Donji Ivancici - Gradina (trig point 1121) Ninici - Borak; Konjsko (trig point 1022, trig point 1032) Dusevine. "I congratulate all participants on successes in operations up to now and wish you much success in further work." Below we have command. I can't see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look. I believe one can see it.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Brigadier-General Enver Hadzihasanovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The things you read out from the document, does it correspond to the events at the time, this being October, November, and the end of that year?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the witness just confirmed that it is as stated in the document, that there was fighting at those positions and he also mentioned certain further actions mentioned in the document as well as the congratulations for the previous successes mentioned, I would like to tender this document as evidence concerning the activities of the fall in 1994 which were offensive actions on the part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as clearly visible from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D290, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, to conclude I wanted to ask you this. You were educated in Sarajevo. You lived in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the geographical layout, which are the dominant features or elevations concerning Ilidza, Vogosca, the centre of Sarajevo, Novo Sarajevo, Nedzarici, Rajlovac? Can you tell us about those, since I believe you were able to notice that while living in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I had hesitated, but since my learned friend has now said that: "Since you were able to notice that while living in Sarajevo," I understand that the witness lived in Ilijas throughout his life and also during the war. And Ilijas, I understand, is some 20 kilometres from Sarajevo. So it may be that he visited Sarajevo and saw one, but to suggest that because he lived there he should know about these specific locations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, where did you live, Witness? Did you live in Sarajevo or in Ilijas or in both places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lived in the municipality of Ilijas and I went to school in Sarajevo. It's my town. I'm well-acquainted with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, can you please tell us to which town does Ilijas belong?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Ilijas is part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you never lived anywhere else, other than in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, can you answer this question, in view of where you lived, this question relating to the dominant features in reference to all of these places that I mentioned so that I don't have to mention them again.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mojmilo, Zuc, Hum, Igman, Trebevic, that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please tell us which forces at that time were at those positions in terms of the features, if you know, or if you know the positions of the -- or if this is something that you know from being in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: From what I know, everything except Trebevic was held by the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovacevic. My name is Manoj Sachdeva, and I'm a lawyer for the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you a few questions today. Can I just get an understanding from you. You -- while you were with the Ilijas Brigade, you served at Nisici plateau. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The whole road from Nisici to Semizovac, all of that constitutes the Nisici plateau, and that's where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And roughly speaking, from the area of, let's say, Skenderija, in the centre of Sarajevo, the place where you served was roughly 20, 20 kilometres towards the north-west. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And which -- well, let me ask you this. How many battalions did the Ilijas Brigade consist of?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, three or four I think but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the battalion that you mentioned earlier, I think it was the 1st, the 1st Battalion, was that the battalion you were part of?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Srednje Battalion, I was a member of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that battalion, how many companies did it have?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Three companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that each company had roughly 100 men. Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: 80 men in my company and I think approximately the -- that number in the other two companies, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in the company that you were part of, were you -- you told the Court that you were a soldier, an infantry person on the -- in the trenches. I take it you didn't have any role within the company or were you -- for example, you weren't the company commander, were you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was a fighter in the trenches throughout the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that you were -- you talked about the weapons. I think you were speaking with respect to the brigade, but when you were talking about the semi-automatic and automatic rifles and a few mortars, I think you also mentioned a howitzer and a tank. Were those weapons part of your company and your battalion, or were you speaking with respect to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It belonged to the Nisici plateau. Perhaps several battalions used it at the time, but that's about how many there were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in your company -- well, you were issued with semi-automatic and automatic rifles. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that that would be the same for your colleagues within your company?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In your company did you also have mortars?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not in the company. Like I said, it didn't just belong to my company. The artillery section covered that whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it that if your company, if it was required -- if the use of mortars and artillery were required, they would have been able to draw upon artillery support. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the mortars, just to ask you about the mortars. I take it you had 120-millimetre mortars, 82-millimetre mortars, and 60-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that the commander of the brigade was Dragan Josipovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you left the brigade in November 1994?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was there not somebody called Milos Delic, who was also the brigade commander at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would change as time went by. Josipovic moved to the Sarajevo 3rd, I think, and I don't know about Milos Delic -- well, it wasn't really that important to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But I just want to establish that the time -- that during the time you were within the Ilijas Brigade, Dragan Josipovic was your -- was the brigade commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with Dragan Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I would see him. Sometimes he would tour the trenches where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you earlier gave evidence about the -- and I'm sorry that I'm jumping a bit, but I just want to ask you this question. You were talking about the 15th of June, 1995. Do you remember that? And I know I'm moving on to your time in the 1st Romanija Brigade and I'm going to ask you some questions about that later, but I just wanted to ask you this question. You remember giving evidence about the 15th of June, 1995. You talked about lightning being struck against you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I think you said that -- that you were -- at least in military terms, you were outnumbered by ten to one.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do I understand it correctly that the next day or pretty soon after the attack by the ABiH you -- the SRK, you managed to regain control of that -- of the Srednje road. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that the morale was high and with a lot of artillery support, this is how you said you managed to regain the territory. I just wanted to ask you what kind of artillery support were you able to draw upon in regaining control?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The artillery was the howitzers, tanks, and mortars. I didn't say that the morale was high. We motivated. There was nowhere for us to go. We had our children behind us, and as far as we were concerned we just had to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, in respect to the morale I'm just reading what you -- what you have said, but never mind. You talked about howitzers, mortars, tanks. How many mortars are we speaking about and what types of mortars?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I was in the trenches the whole time. I wasn't where the artillery was. The mortars were 120-millimetres and 80-millimetres. The tanks were old. I don't know what their markings were, but there were plenty of artillery weapons. I don't know exactly which ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. So I take it that with the plenty of artillery weapons that you had, in spite of the fact that you were outnumbered by ten to one, the SRK still managed to gain the military upper hand. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We simply had to defend ourselves. I don't know if we were in the position of having the upper hand. We were carrying defensive actions, not offensive actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, in that combat activity on the 15th of June when you were outnumbered by ten to one, it's right, is it not, that the SRK managed to regain control of that strategic road. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, while you were with the Ilijas Brigade -- well, let me ask you this. Do you know of a place called Breza?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And at the time that you were with the Ilijas Brigade, I take it that Breza was controlled -- well, it was within the territory of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can I put it this way, that Breza was, let us say, part of your military -- I won't say your military area of responsibility because I'm obviously speaking about an area that is not in SRK control. But it was important for your brigade to -- to understand what military movements there might have been in Breza and the other surrounding municipalities. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, in fact, during these combat activities, the forces within the Ilijas Brigade would -- would trade shots or would fire on to Breza. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. The positions of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were precisely these ones, on the boundary between Breza and Ilijas, and it's possible that there was -- yes, there was firing along the line of separation, but there were more combat actions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last part of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to repeat the last part of what you said because the interpreter didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The line of separation between Ilijas and Breza was more towards the Ilijas municipality territory. So there was no need to hit the Breza municipality area except for what was on the line of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There may have been no need in your -- that's your evidence, but can I suggest to you that on occasion the town of Breza was fired upon -- was fired upon by soldiers within the Ilijas Brigade. Do you accept that possibility?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If there was a military target involved, I do accept that, but there was no deliberate firing, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So when you say if there was a military target involved, so in other words there could have been, for example, a tank -- hypothetically there could have been a tank in the town of Breza, and that would -- that would then result in fire from the SRK into the town of Breza. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If artillery weapons are pin-pointed, you would not need the whole of the SRK to shell Breza. If somebody fired from that area, though, it was logical to respond to such fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't mean the whole of the SRK, and I'm sorry for my imprecise question. Of course I refer to the forces in the Ilijas Brigade. Let me ask you this: It was the case that the battalion commanders, and indeed the brigade commanders, would hand down certain targets -- target lists to their soldiers, their subordinates. Is that right? In other words, targets -- targets to be engaged would be communicated to those persons who were to engage targets from the command?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Artillery perhaps, yes, but I was a fighter and my target was clear: An enemy in front of you within the range of my rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. So with respect to artillery, if there were targets to be engaged by tanks or by howitzers and also by mortars, those targets would be communicated from -- from the brigade commander down to his subordinates. Do I have a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If a target was noted, then that would then come from the command. I mean, I wasn't an artillery man, but I assume that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.42 p.m.,
